analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance to cover over-the-counter birth control pills without copays.
analysis.headline: A bill to require insurance coverage of over-the-counter birth control gathered 35 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, but died in committee without ever getting a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private health insurance plans to cover over-the-counter (OTC) birth control pills approved by the FDA, with no copays, deductibles, or prescription needed — extending the existing Affordable Care Act birth control coverage rule to nonprescription pills. It also would have barred retailers that stock OTC pills from interfering with a customer's ability to buy them or get accurate information about them. It was referred to the Senate health committee in May 2022 and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who use birth control — the bill's own findings cite roughly 72 million women of reproductive age and a survey finding that 1 in 3 women has struggled to afford birth control at some point, leading to inconsistent use. If the FDA approved a pill for OTC sale, insurance would have to pay for it with no out-of-pocket cost and no doctor's visit to get a prescription.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women who struggle to afford birth control

how_it_helps.text: Requires the health, labor, and treasury departments to clarify that private plans must cover FDA-approved over-the-counter contraceptives even without a prescription, extending the existing no-cost-sharing birth control benefit.
Prohibits retailers that stock OTC daily-use birth control pills from interfering with a customer's access to the pills or to medically accurate information about them.

States the Senate's view that easier access and affordability must go together — that making birth control easier to get but leaving it unaffordable 'is to leave unacceptable barriers in place' — and urges drug makers to seek FDA approval for OTC sale.

The bill's findings cite 62.1 million women already covered by the ACA birth control benefit and 1 in 3 women reporting they have struggled to afford birth control, using it inconsistently as a result.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers funding group plans would bear the cost of covering OTC contraceptives without cost-sharing, a cost that can flow into premiums. Retailers stocking OTC pills would take on a new legal duty not to obstruct access.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to people with private insurance; the bill expressly allows a retailer to refuse to sell OTC pills to someone who cannot pay for them, so it does not solve affordability for the uninsured.

Because plans would have to cover a new category of products with no cost-sharing, the added cost would land on insurers and employer plans and could feed into premiums paid by all enrollees — the coverage requirement itself is what the bill mandates.
The bill does nothing to change the FDA approval process; OTC availability depends on a manufacturer voluntarily applying for and winning FDA approval, which the bill can only urge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women with private insurance, the benefit is concrete: no copay and no prescription visit for OTC pills, removing two of the most common barriers to consistent use. The main cost is a modest coverage expansion for insurers and employer plans that could nudge premiums upward, and the bill leaves the uninsured relying on the retail price. It is a targeted access bill, not a sweeping one, and its main weakness is that it depends entirely on a manufacturer first winning FDA approval for an OTC pill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in May 2022, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Patty Murray on May 26, 2022, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

The bill drew 35 cosponsors — 34 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents — but no further action was ever taken on it, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and retailers were spared a new coverage mandate and access duty. Women hoping for no-cost OTC birth control gained nothing from the bill's death, though FDA approval of an OTC pill could still happen separately.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and retailers; OTC pill users gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 35 cosponsors, all from her party's caucus and the chamber's independents.

for.name: 34 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making support a majority of the Senate Democratic caucus plus the chamber's one independent cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's sponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 26, 2022 and never held a markup or advanced it before the Congress ended.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 50 Republican senators cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no Republican support at any point.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: 34 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents signed on, while none of the 50 Republicans did; the bill never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required private plans to cover FDA-approved OTC contraceptives with no cost-sharing and no prescription, adding a new category to the ACA preventive-services mandate they already administer. Insurers' interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the access the bill offered women.

An over-the-counter switch would open a retail market for their pills, and the bill's insurance mandate would guarantee that insured customers pay nothing out of pocket. The bill explicitly urged manufacturers to seek FDA approval for OTC sale.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and retailers stocking OTC pills
industries.note: Retailers would have faced a legal duty not to interfere with a customer's purchase of or information about OTC birth control. The burden is narrow — the bill still let them refuse a customer who could not pay — but it removes retailer discretion over access.
